title: Learning Boolean juntas from uniform random examples
formal: Does there exist one uniform classical randomized learner \(A\) and universal positive integers \(B,C\) such that every Boolean \(k\)-junta on \(n\) variables can be learned from independent uniform noiseless examples in time polynomial in \(n,2^k\) and inverse error? Explicitly, for all integers \(n\ge1\), \(0\le k\le n\), \(t\ge3\), and every \(k\)-junta \(f:\{0,1\}^n\to\{0,1\}\), the learner receives \(1^n,1^k,1^t\) and an independent-example oracle \(\operatorname{EX}_f\). Every execution takes at most \(B(n+2^k+t)^C\) steps and outputs an ordinary Boolean circuit \(h\) for which \[\Pr_{A,\,\operatorname{EX}_f}\left[\Pr_{x\sim U_n}[h(x)\ne f(x)]\le\frac1t\right]\ge\frac23.\] The exponent \(C\), constant \(B\) and machine are independent of \(n,k,t,f\). This preserves the existing full \(\operatorname{poly}(n,2^k,1/\varepsilon)\) target; it is not merely a separate polynomial-time statement for every fixed \(k\).
definitions:
Write \([n]=\{1,\ldots,n\}\). A \(k\)-junta is a Boolean function for which there exist an unknown subset \(S=\{i_1<\cdots<i_r\}\subseteq[n]\), \(r\le k\), and an arbitrary Boolean table \(g:\{0,1\}^r\to\{0,1\}\) such that \[f(x)=g(x_{i_1},\ldots,x_{i_r})\quad\text{for all }x\in\{0,1\}^n.\] Neither \(S\) nor \(g\) is given to the learner. No monotonicity, sparsity of the truth table or lower bound on variable influence is assumed. For \(k=0\), the class consists of the two constant functions, using the unique empty input to \(g\). The public \(k\) is only an upper bound on the number of relevant coordinates; it need not be the minimal support size.

\(U_n\) gives each binary vector probability \(2^{-n}\). Each call to \(\operatorname{EX}_f\) supplies a new pair \((x,f(x))\) with \(x\sim U_n\), independent of all previous draws and the learner’s fair random coins. The unknown target is fixed before the data are drawn. The learner can request further independent examples adaptively, but cannot choose their inputs, obtain membership-query labels, or request coupled or neighboring examples. Labels are exact noiseless bits. The outer probability measures confidence over the complete learning execution; the inner probability is zero-one prediction error on a fresh independent input. Reciprocals of positive integers suffice to represent arbitrary desired positive error tolerances up to polynomial rounding overhead. The fixed confidence is \(2/3\).

The output is a finite acyclic ordinary Boolean circuit on the \(n\) input bits, using two-input AND/OR gates, one-input NOT gates and constants with a fixed effective binary encoding. It may depend on all coordinates and need not itself be a \(k\)-junta; this is improper learning. It is evaluated without the training oracle and with no stored target-dependent state other than its output description. The learner is a probabilistic multitape Turing machine, with no advice, receiving the displayed public integers in unary. All example reading, computation, stored-data access, fair random bits and output writing count in the worst-case bit-time bound, which also bounds the number of example requests and output length. The example generator’s internal sampling cost is not charged. Circuit evaluation is polynomial in the written circuit size under this encoding. Repeated access to stored examples and any polynomial amount of memory within the time bound are allowed. The requirement is predictive approximation; it does not require identifying the exact relevant set, giving a minimum representation or recovering every truth-table entry.

Polynomial dependence on \(2^k\) permits an exponential dependence on the number of relevant variables, since an arbitrary \(k\)-bit table already has \(2^k\) entries. It excludes a degree of \(n\) that grows with \(k\). For every fixed \(c>0\), the displayed guarantee would in particular be polynomial in \(n,t\) for all \(k\le c\log_2 n\); an algorithm that only handles each constant \(k\) with its own exponent need not satisfy it. The accuracy target is the explicitly bounded rational error \(1/t\); the problem asks for exact existence of the learner and universal exponent rather than a numerical optimal value.
answer_criterion: Give a Lean-checked proof that such \(A,B,C\) exist, or prove the complete negation: for every proposed uniform machine and universal constants, some allowed \(n,k,t,f\) violates the worst-case resource bound, finite hypothesis condition or the stated PAC probability. A positive answer must handle all Boolean junta tables and all support sizes up to \(n\) with one exponent independent of \(k\). A learner using membership queries, correlated random-walk examples, a randomly perturbed marginal distribution, or only monotone targets does not meet the specified interface. A statistical-query, limited-memory or specified-neural-training lower bound does not exclude every allowed machine. Conditional cryptographic hardness must retain its unproved premise and is not the unconditional negation. Neither exact support recovery nor a prescribed proper output is an additional obligation.
why: Determine whether arbitrary dependence on a small hidden set of variables can be learned efficiently from ordinary observations, separating computational search from sample sufficiency.

importance.reason: A central unresolved task in computational learning theory, isolating feature selection and serving as a prerequisite for efficient learning of general decision trees and DNF formulas.

progress.text: Mossel–O’Donnell–Servedio publish the first constant-factor improvement over the brute-force exponent for learning arbitrary juntas from uniform examples.
Valiant’s FOCS work and JACM version improve noiseless junta learning to roughly \(n^{0.6k}\), using fast correlation algorithms.
Beretta’s revised RANDOM paper distinguishes junta-distribution learning from noiseless function learning and records the continuing computational gap.
Servedio’s survey explicitly retains the uniform-example junta barrier and contrasts it with efficient learning using membership queries.
A new gradient-based learning result uses labelled samples from a lazy random walk; its temporal dependence is outside the independent-example model.

The original OpenReview pointer is now verified as the NeurIPS paper on externally smoothed Markov random fields. Its positive theorem requires that random smoothing and does not cover the exact uniform marginal as a worst-case instance.

Rechecked the established exponents, full smoothed-distribution and random-walk theorem interfaces, and the inherited textbook milestone. The exact universal polynomial target and importance score are unchanged; bounded checks found no matching resolution.

status_note: The checked 2025 survey and NeurIPS introduction retain the independent-uniform-example junta barrier. The inherited OpenReview pointer was identified on 16 September 2026 as Chandrasekaran–Klivans, Learning Juntas under Markov Random Fields; its full theorem has a positive random-smoothing premise, with probability over that perturbation and the stated graph/width conditions. The checked May 2026 theorem uses correlated lazy-random-walk examples. Neither matches the exact passive uniform model. Bounded checks through 16 September 2026 found no general learner or unconditional lower bound for the retained universal polynomial target, so current status remains uncertain.

context_blocks.text: A junta uses only a few of the available input features, but its dependence on those features can be completely arbitrary. The problem asks for an efficient predictor from passive observations. It separates the small information content of the hidden rule from the computational cost of locating useful features among many irrelevant ones.

The finite class contains at most \((k+1)n^k2^{2^k}\) functions. At constant confidence, realizable finite-class learning therefore needs only \(O((2^k+k\log(n+1)+\log(k+1)+1)/\varepsilon)\) examples information-theoretically. This fits the desired polynomial resource scale; the unresolved requirement is efficient computation with those examples.

Mossel–O’Donnell–Servedio give exact learning in \(n^{(\omega/(\omega+1))k}\operatorname{poly}(n,2^k,\log(1/\delta))\) time, where \(\omega\) is a valid matrix-multiplication exponent. Using the exponent available in their paper gives roughly \(n^{0.704k}\) times polynomial factors. Their model uses independent uniform examples, so this is progress in the required access model.

Valiant’s Corollary 7 improves noiseless junta learning to a bound below \(n^{0.60k}\operatorname{poly}(n,2^k)\) for the matrix-multiplication exponent and constants used there. Servedio’s November 2025 survey still reports the roughly \(n^{0.6k}\) benchmark. The exponent of the ambient dimension continues to grow with support size, so this is not the universal polynomial in the formal statement.

Individual-coordinate correlation can vanish even for a relevant coordinate, as in the parity of three selected bits. That illustrates a limitation of certain correlation statistics, not an unconditional lower bound against all example-based learners: noiseless parity itself has an efficient algebraic learner. Statistical-query restrictions must remain distinct from unrestricted observation of the actual samples.

Membership-query algorithms and monotone-junta learners have stronger positive guarantees under their respective conditions. Membership queries let the learner choose which inputs are labeled, while monotonicity restricts the possible truth tables. Neither condition is assumed here.

Beretta’s RANDOM 2025 paper concerns distributions whose probability mass function depends on a small coordinate set and relates that density-learning task to sparse noisy parity. Its introduction separately describes the persistent difficulty of noiseless Boolean function learning under uniform examples. The distribution-learning equivalence is not a resolution of this card’s prediction problem.

The inherited OpenReview pointer has now been identified as Chandrasekaran–Klivans, Learning Juntas under Markov Random Fields, NeurIPS 2025. Its introduction explicitly retains the difficult uniform-example question. Its positive Theorem 1.3 assumes a smoothed Markov random field, a known bounded-degree dependency graph and the stated bounded-width parameters, with success probability also taken over the random external-field perturbation. Even though the unperturbed uniform distribution is a Markov random field, a guarantee over positive random smoothing does not imply a guarantee at that exact unperturbed distribution.

Cornacchia–Mikulincer–Mossel’s May 2026 Theorem 2 studies labeled samples along a lazy random walk on the hypercube. It gives nearly linear ambient-dimension sample dependence for each fixed support size, with the stated target-dependent constants. Consecutive examples are correlated even if each has a uniform marginal. An independent-example source does not provide that temporal information, so the theorem concerns a different learning interface.

A \(k\)-junta has a decision-tree or DNF representation of size at most \(2^k\) under the usual leaf/term convention, with polynomial overhead if literal occurrences are counted. Efficient uniform-example learning for those larger representation classes would therefore imply the requested bound. This explains the junta problem’s role as a basic obstacle within computational learning theory.

Wigderson’s Open Problem 17.9, inherited through the user-approved consolidation of TCS-0023, asks for polynomial-time uniform learning beyond constant support size, or hardness under a natural complexity assumption. The retained card asks for the specific stronger bound \(\operatorname{poly}(n,2^k,1/\varepsilon)\) for every \(k\). A positive answer handles \(k=O(\log n)\); success only in a slower-growing regime or a conditional negative answer is not the same assertion. This historical source remains a related milestone, and the earlier consolidation and reserved identifier are preserved as provenance.

The output may be any efficient Boolean circuit and need not recover the exact relevant set.
Known faster-exponent algorithms and results using smoothing, monotonicity, membership queries or correlated examples do not meet this full guarantee.
